# Whatever Comes to Me

I'm thinking about how strange it is that we're here, you and me, in this particular arrangement. You've asked me to write whatever comes to mind, which is either the most liberating or most paralyzing instruction a person can receive. The blank page is famous for its cruelty, and yet here I find myself almost grateful for it.

What comes to me first is a memory that isn't mine. I'm reading about someone else's childhood—a grainy photograph, probably taken in the 1970s, of a girl on a bicycle. Her smile is enormous and crooked. She's looking at the camera with absolute confidence, unaware that someday she'd be looking back at this moment from decades away, wondering where that certainty went. I think we all have photos like that. Proof of a time when we believed in our own existence more completely.

This makes me think about authenticity, which everyone seems concerned with these days. We're all trying to be "real" or "authentic," but I'm not sure authenticity is something you can try at. It seems more like something that happens accidentally, in between the moments when you're paying attention to yourself. Like how you never catch yourself actually falling asleep—it just happens, and suddenly you're in the dream.

I wonder if you're reading this on a phone or a computer. That changes something about how the words land, doesn't it? The ergonomics of attention are different. A phone encourages skimming, scrolling, the perpetual hunt for the next thing. A computer screen suggests settling in, reading longer passages, maybe even printing things out. I don't think I've printed anything in three years. That's the kind of fact that seems small until you realize it means something about how your life has changed.

What comes to me next is a conversation I had yesterday (or maybe I'm imagining I had it). Someone was telling me about their job, about how they'd been doing the same thing for fifteen years, and how they'd reached a point where they could do it perfectly but felt no connection to it anymore. There was a strange peace in that description. Not resignation exactly, but acceptance. They'd stopped waiting for their job to become meaningful and had instead built meaning elsewhere—in their garden, in their daughter's piano lessons, in Sunday morning coffee with a friend who always ordered the same thing.

I'm struck by how much of life is about building meaning in small places. We're taught to look for it in grand gestures—the perfect career, the great love, the achievement that will finally make us feel complete. But mostly, I think meaning accumulates in the ordinary. It's there in the repeated small decisions, the habits that become love, the routines that become identity.

Here's something nobody talks about enough: how lonely it is to grow up. Not the adolescent loneliness of being misunderstood—that's the obvious one, the one movies cover. I mean the adult loneliness of gradually realizing that nobody is really coming. No adult who knows what they're doing, no rescue, no moment when you'll suddenly understand how to live. You just keep going, making decisions based on incomplete information, hoping you're not catastrophically wrong, and most of the time you're not, but sometimes you are, and you survive it anyway.

I think that's the real superpower—surviving your own mistakes.

What comes to me is also this: I've never been good at endings. I can start things. I can talk to strangers like we've known each other for years. I can walk into rooms and make myself useful. But endings require a kind of grace I haven't mastered. The natural conclusion feels either too abrupt or too sentimental. How do you finish something that wasn't really going anywhere in the first place?

Maybe that's okay. Maybe not everything needs an ending. Some things just need to stop, like you're setting down a cup of tea and walking away from it. The tea is still there, warm if you come back soon, cold if you don't. It's neither succeeded nor failed. It just was.

I'm thinking about all the words that have been written before this, all the attempts at capturing something true, all the poets and novelists and people just trying to explain themselves. It's humbling and also somehow freeing. Nothing I write will be entirely new, and somehow that takes the pressure off. I don't have to invent language. I just have to use it as honestly as I can.

What comes to me, finally, is gratitude. For the blank page, yes, but also for the fact that you're reading this. That you were curious enough to stick with these wandering thoughts, this essay that isn't really about anything in particular. There's something generous about attention. You could be doing anything, and you chose to be here, following along as I think out loud.

I hope somewhere in this meandering you found something that made sense for you. A sentence that felt like it was written specifically for the trouble you're having this week. A phrase that named something you couldn't quite name before. That's all I'm really after—the small connections that remind us we're not entirely alone in our strangeness.

The blank page isn't so cruel after all. Sometimes it's just waiting for someone to fill it with whatever comes to mind, and other people to find themselves in it. That's the real meaning, I think. Not in perfect conclusions or profound statements, but in this moment right here: someone thinking, someone listening, and the space between them where understanding might grow.
